_comment: The single country table. Stage one scores a route from the band weights; stage two rates the premium from the band factors. Before this file each stage kept its own list and they disagreed: Morocco was high risk for the premium and band B for the score, Czechia was medium for the premium and band A for the score, and eighteen countries could be assessed but not quoted.
reviewNote: Simplified teaching tiers, not an underwriting rating. Re-check before each course: a band that is right today can be wrong after a sanctions package or a conflict.
methodology: Each country sits in one of four bands. The band combines the reliability of its logistics and customs (World Bank LPI), its maritime and inland security exposure (ICC-IMB piracy reporting and the Lloyd’s Joint War Committee listed areas), and whether it is under trade sanctions. Stage one averages the two ends, because cargo is exposed at both. Stage two takes the worse of the two, because that is how a rate is set.

C.label: Medium
C.note: Caution advised — check documentation and transit times.

D.label: High
D.note: Enhanced coverage needed. Political or security exposure.

notes.Russia: Band D on sanctions, not on infrastructure. Trade restrictions, payment channels and insurance availability are the binding constraints.
notes.Ukraine: Band D. Active conflict; Black Sea routings and port availability change faster than any annual index can track.
notes.Lebanon: Band D. Economic collapse and conflict exposure; Beirut port capacity remains reduced since 2020.
notes.Libya: Band D. Fragmented governance and unreliable port operations.
notes.Egypt: Band C. The country score is only part of the story: since late 2023 many carriers have routed around the Cape rather than transit the Red Sea, which lengthens transit and changes where the cargo is exposed.
notes.Saudi Arabia: Moved from C to B in the September 2026 review. Sustained port investment and a clear LPI improvement. The Red Sea exposure is a corridor question, not a country one.
notes.Oman: Moved from D to B in the September 2026 review. The old D reflected the Gulf of Aden, not Oman itself — Salalah and Sohar are well-run hubs. The corridor risk belongs to the water, not the flag.
notes.India: Moved from C to B in the September 2026 review. India rose sharply in the 2023 LPI, helped by port turnaround times and the dedicated freight corridors.
notes.Nigeria: Moved from D to C in the September 2026 review. The IMB has reported a sustained fall in Gulf of Guinea incidents since 2021. Inland security and port congestion keep it above band B.
notes.Mauritania: Moved from D to C in the September 2026 review. Limited logistics capacity, but no armed conflict or sanctions driver to justify the top band.
notes.France: Moved from B to A in the September 2026 review. Its LPI sits with Germany and the Netherlands; the old B was an inconsistency, not a judgement.

sources.label: Logistics Performance Index
sources.informs: Customs, infrastructure and the reliability of transit times. Drives most movements between bands A, B and C.

sources.label: Piracy and Armed Robbery Against Ships
sources.informs: Maritime security exposure. The IMB counts actual and attempted attacks by location, which is why the exposure follows corridors rather than flags.

sources.label: Listed Areas — Hull, War, Strikes, Terrorism and Related Perils
sources.publisher: Lloyd’s Market Association, Joint War Committee
sources.informs: The reference underwriters actually use to decide where war risk is rated separately. Worth showing students: it is a list of waters, not of countries.

sources.label: EU Sanctions Map
sources.informs: Whether trade with a country is restricted. A sanctions listing places a country in band D on its own, whatever its infrastructure.

sources.label: Review of Maritime Transport
sources.informs: Trade volumes, fleet and the pressure on chokepoints such as Suez, Bab el-Mandeb, Malacca and Panama.
